Pregnancy

Prenatal Visit Schedule: Week by Week Appointment Guide

Updated: August 5, 2026

Written and edited by Mohammadamin Namyar, founder of BeMama — checked against published guidance from recognized health organizations.

A typical prenatal visit schedule starts with a first appointment around 8 weeks of pregnancy, then repeats every 4 weeks until 28 weeks, every 2 weeks until 36 weeks, and weekly until birth. That adds up to about 10 to 15 visits in a standard low-risk pregnancy. This guide lays out the timetable week by week, what happens at each stage, and how the pattern changes when a pregnancy needs closer watching.

The standard rhythm at a glance

In a typical low-risk pregnancy, the schedule looks like this: a first visit around 8 weeks, then a visit about every 4 weeks until 28 weeks, every 2 weeks from 28 to 36 weeks, and every week from 36 weeks until your baby is born. Counted out, that comes to roughly 10 to 15 appointments over the whole pregnancy. This is the pattern most obstetricians and midwives in the United States and Canada follow, and it matches the guidance professional groups such as ACOG publish. Your clinic may shift a visit by a week here or there, and that is normal.

The spacing is not random. Visits are far apart early on because a healthy pregnancy changes slowly in the middle months, then they tighten as blood pressure problems, growth concerns, and labor questions become more likely. Some practices offer a few visits by phone or video, and some low-risk care models use slightly fewer in-person appointments. None of that should worry you. What matters is that someone is checking the same core signs on a regular rhythm. If you miss a visit, call and rebook rather than waiting for the next scheduled one, since some checks work best inside a specific window of weeks.

Weeks 8 to 13: the first visit and early screening

Call the clinic as soon as you have a positive test, because many offices book several weeks out. The first visit usually lands around 8 weeks and is the longest of the whole schedule. Expect a full health history, questions about medications, past pregnancies, and family conditions, plus a physical exam and a panel of blood and urine tests that check blood type, iron, immunity, and infections. Most people also have a dating ultrasound at or near this visit. That early scan confirms how far along you are and sets the due date every later appointment is measured against, which is why this visit anchors the rest of the timetable.

From 10 weeks onward you can choose cell-free DNA screening, often called NIPT, a blood test that screens for certain chromosome conditions. Some clinics also offer a combined first-trimester screen with an ultrasound and blood work between 11 and 13 weeks. Both are optional, and it is fine to take a visit to think them over. One more thing about timing: if you have bleeding, strong pain, a chronic condition such as diabetes or high blood pressure, or a history of pregnancy complications, ask to be seen earlier than the standard 8 weeks. Clinics expect those calls and can usually fit you in sooner.

Weeks 14 to 27: the monthly stretch

Through the middle of pregnancy you will usually be seen once a month, around weeks 16, 20, and 24, give or take. These visits are shorter than the first one. Your clinician checks blood pressure, tests urine, listens to the fetal heartbeat, and, from about 20 weeks, measures fundal height, the distance from your pubic bone to the top of the uterus, to follow growth. Somewhere in this stretch most people start feeling movement, usually between 16 and 24 weeks, often closer to 20 in a first pregnancy, and visits become a natural place to ask about anything that feels new, from round ligament pain to sleep position.

Two big milestones sit in this window. The anatomy scan, a detailed ultrasound of your baby's organs, spine, and placenta, happens between 18 and 22 weeks, and many clinics can tell you the sex then if you want to know. Between 24 and 28 weeks comes the glucose screen for gestational diabetes, a sugary drink followed by a blood draw. Around 28 weeks your blood count is often rechecked for anemia, and if your blood type is Rh negative you will usually be offered an Rh immune globulin injection. Each of these has its own guide on this site if you want the details before the day arrives.

Week 28 to birth: visits speed up

From 28 weeks, visits move to every 2 weeks, usually around weeks 28, 30, 32, 34, and 36. The checks stay familiar, but attention shifts toward blood pressure, swelling, headaches, and how the baby is growing and moving, because problems such as preeclampsia become more common in the third trimester. This is also the window for the Tdap vaccine, offered between 27 and 36 weeks in each pregnancy to pass whooping cough protection to your baby. Seasonal vaccines like the flu shot can be given whenever they are due. Keep raising anything odd at these visits; late pregnancy is when small changes matter most.

From 36 weeks you will be seen weekly until birth. Around 36 to 37 weeks your clinician does the group B strep swab, a quick test that decides whether you need antibiotics in labor. Weekly visits check the baby's position, since a breech baby at this stage opens a conversation about options, and your clinician may offer a cervical check near your due date, which you can accept or decline. If you pass 40 to 41 weeks, expect extra monitoring, such as a nonstress test or a fluid check, and a talk about when induction makes sense. The schedule ends when labor begins.

The same checks every time, and why your schedule might differ

Almost every routine visit repeats a short ritual: blood pressure, a urine sample, weight, fundal height once you are far enough along, and a listen to the fetal heartbeat. Each piece earns its place. Blood pressure and urine protein together watch for preeclampsia, urine can also flag silent infections, fundal height tracks growth between ultrasounds, and the heartbeat confirms the baby is doing well. The repetition is the point, because a change from your own baseline is more telling than any single number. It helps to jot down readings, symptoms, and questions between visits, in the BeMama app or a small notebook, so patterns are easy to show your clinician.

Some pregnancies need a closer watch. Twins or higher multiples, chronic conditions such as diabetes, high blood pressure, or thyroid disease, age 35 and up, and a history of preterm birth or preeclampsia all commonly mean extra visits, extra ultrasounds, or added monitoring in the third trimester. Your clinician should explain your version of the schedule early on. And between any two visits, call the clinic the same day for bleeding, leaking fluid, a severe headache, vision changes, regular contractions before 37 weeks, or a clear drop in movement after 28 weeks. For heavy bleeding, severe belly pain, or any symptom that feels like an emergency, go to the nearest emergency department rather than waiting for a call back. Do not save urgent symptoms for the next appointment; the schedule is a floor, not a ceiling.

Evidence-informed guidance

What trusted health organizations recommend

Prenatal care is individualized rather than a single universal calendar. Visits, laboratory tests, ultrasound, screening choices, and monitoring depend on gestational age, health history, local practice, and concerns that arise.

Screening tests estimate the chance of a condition, while diagnostic tests are used to confirm or exclude specific problems. A prenatal professional can explain what a result means and what choices follow.

How BeMama can help

Use BeMama to record appointments, test names, instructions, and questions. The educational schedule in the app does not replace the plan from your own doctor or midwife.

When to seek help

Do not wait for the next scheduled visit when you have an urgent symptom or a significant change in fetal movement.

Sources and further reading

  • ACOG — Routine Tests During Pregnancy
  • ACOG — Ultrasound Exams

Links lead directly to guidance from the organizations named above.

Key takeaways

  • Expect a first visit around 8 weeks, then visits every 4 weeks until 28 weeks, every 2 weeks until 36, and weekly until birth.
  • A typical low-risk pregnancy involves about 10 to 15 prenatal appointments in total.
  • Key windows: anatomy scan at 18 to 22 weeks, glucose screen at 24 to 28, Tdap at 27 to 36, group B strep swab at 36 to 37.
  • Every visit repeats the same core checks: blood pressure, urine, fundal height, and the fetal heartbeat.
  • Twins, chronic conditions, or age 35 and up usually mean more visits, and new symptoms deserve a call between appointments.

Frequently asked questions

How often are prenatal appointments?

In a low-risk pregnancy, prenatal appointments happen about every 4 weeks until 28 weeks, every 2 weeks from 28 to 36 weeks, and weekly from 36 weeks until birth. The first visit is usually around 8 weeks. Twins, chronic conditions, or complications usually mean more frequent visits, so your own calendar may be busier.

When is the first prenatal appointment?

The first prenatal appointment is usually around 8 weeks of pregnancy, counted from the first day of your last period. Call to book as soon as you have a positive test, since clinics often schedule weeks ahead. Ask to be seen sooner if you have bleeding, pain, a chronic condition, or past pregnancy complications.

How many prenatal visits are there during pregnancy?

Most low-risk pregnancies include about 10 to 15 prenatal visits from the first appointment to birth. The total depends on when care starts, how your clinic spaces visits, and whether anything needs closer follow-up. Higher-risk pregnancies often add appointments in the third trimester.

What happens at each prenatal visit?

Every routine visit includes blood pressure, a urine check, weight, the fetal heartbeat, and, from mid-pregnancy, a fundal height measurement. Certain weeks then add extras: a dating ultrasound early on, the anatomy scan at 18 to 22 weeks, the glucose screen at 24 to 28, Tdap at 27 to 36, and the group B strep swab at 36 to 37. There is always time to ask questions, so bring them.

This article is general education, not medical advice, diagnosis, or treatment. Always talk with a qualified healthcare professional about your situation, and seek urgent care for emergencies.
